paragraphs.heading: Energy per unit of charge
paragraphs.text: Electric potential is the electric potential energy a charged particle has at some location, divided by that particle's charge. Put simply, it is energy per unit of charge. It is measured in joules per coulomb, a unit called the volt, named in honor of Alessandro Volta. That is why the potential difference between two points is known as a voltage.

paragraphs.heading: Work to move a test charge
paragraphs.text: Another way to see it is as the work needed to carry a test charge from a reference point to a chosen spot, divided by the charge. The test charge is assumed so small that it barely disturbs the charges making the field, and it is moved so gently that it gains no kinetic energy and gives off no radiation. The reference point has a potential of zero by definition. It is usually the earth or a point infinitely far away, but any point can be used. Because the zero is chosen freely, potential is only fixed up to an added constant.

paragraphs.heading: Potential and energy
paragraphs.text: The potentials at two points tell you how a charged particle's energy changes between them. If a particle with charge q goes from point A to point B, its potential energy changes by q times the change in potential: U_B − U_A = q(V_B − V_A). Dividing out the charge leaves a quantity that belongs to the electric field itself, not to any particular particle.

paragraphs.heading: Like a ball rolling downhill
paragraphs.text: Potential borrows an idea from classical mechanics, which deals with force, energy and potential. When an object moves the way a force pushes it, its potential energy drops. A cannonball at the top of a hill has more gravitational potential energy than at the bottom, and as it rolls down, that energy turns into energy of motion, called kinetic energy. For some force fields, an object's potential energy depends only on where it sits in the field. Gravity is one such field, and the electric field is another, as long as no magnetic field is changing in time.

paragraphs.heading: Around a point charge
paragraphs.text: For a single point charge Q, the potential at a distance r is V_𝐄 = 1/4πε₀Q/r, known as the Coulomb potential. Here ε₀ stands for the permittivity of vacuum. It shrinks with one over the distance, whereas the size of a point charge's field shrinks with one over the distance squared. This potential is continuous everywhere except at the spot where the charge itself sits.

paragraphs.heading: When fields change in time
paragraphs.text: In electrodynamics, where fields change over time, a single potential is no longer enough to describe the electric field. Instead the field is built from the electric potential together with the magnetic vector potential. These two together form a four-vector, and under Lorentz transformations the two kinds of potential mix into each other.

paragraphs.heading: What a voltmeter reads
paragraphs.text: Inside metals, and other solids and liquids, an electron's energy depends not only on the electric potential but also on its local atomic surroundings. A voltmeter connected between two different metals reports the potential difference corrected for those differing surroundings. What it actually measures is the Fermi level of the electrons divided by the electron's charge.
